Curriculum for Endocrinology (SUMMARY from the book) #1

  • 1.Introduction in Endocrinology
  • 2. The endocrine hypothalamus, hypothalamic-hypophysial-portal system
  • 2.1 Growth and puberty
  • 2.2 Normal puberty
  • = process of growth and development that begins during gestation and continues until the end of
  • reproductive life
  • After juvenile pause the hypothalamic pulse generator ↑ activity → ↑ secretion of pituitary gonadotropins
  • and gonadal sex steroids → bring out secondary sexual development, growth spurt, fertility
  • Physical changes
  • FEMALES (8-13 years) MALES (9-14 years)
  • - Breast development = 1st sign of puberty, pubic - ↑ size of testes to >2.5cm in the longest diameter
  • hair development, adrenarche, menarche and testicular volume of ≥ 4ml = first sign of
  • - Development of internal and external genitalia normal puberty
  • - Pubertal growth spurt - Development of internal and external genitalia
  • - Gynoid body fat disposition (fat around the hips, - Pubic hair development, facial + thoracic hair,
  • opposite is called android body fat) adrenarche
  • - Onset of erections
  • - Pubertal growth spurt
  • - Muscle mass development, thickening of voice
  • - Seborrheic, acne skin
  • Pubertal development is classified by Tanner and Marshall in 5 stages:
  • CATEGORY STAGES FEMALE MALE
  • Pubic hair stage P1 No hair
  • P2 Downy hair
  • P3 Scant terminal hair
  • P4 Terminal hair that fills the entire triangle overlying the pubic region
  • P5 Terminal hair that extends beyond the inguinal crease onto the thigh
  • Breast development B1 No glandular breast tissue palpable
  • B2 Breast bud palpable under the areola
  • (1st pubertal sign)
  • B3 Breast tissue palpable outside areola;
  • no areolar development
  • B4 Areola elevated above the contour of
  • the breast, forming a “double scoop”
  • appearance
  • B5 Areolar mound recedes into single
  • breast contour with areolar
  • hyperpigmentation, papillae
  • development, and nipple protrusion
  • External Genitalia stage G1 Testicular volume < 4 ml or long
  • axis < 2.5 cm
  • G2 4 ml-8 ml (or 2.5 to 3.3 cm long)
  • (1st pubertal sign)
  • G3 9 ml-12 ml (or 3.4 to 4.0 cm long)
  • G4 15-20 ml (or 4.1 to 4.5 cm long)
  • G5 > 20 ml (or > 4.5 cm long)

2.3 Delayed / premature (precocious) puberty #2

  • = appearance of secondary sexual development <9 in boys and 7-8 in girls
  • Classification
  • A. Central (complete or true) PP = CPP
  • = premature activation of the HH-gland axis; Fertility is possible
  • Etiology
  • - Familial tendency (constitutional)
  • - CNS disorders: tumors, infectious or granulomatous conditions
  • - Idiopathic
  • Clinical Signs:
  • 1. Precocious secondary sex development
  • FEMALE = at least B2 (Tanner)
  • MALE = at least G2 (testicular enlargement; Tanner)
  • BOTH SEXES = and/or pubic - axillary hair: P2
  • 2. Increased somatic development, growth velocity, skeletal maturation
  • - Tall child growing up to be a short adult = paradox
  • 3. Psychological manifestations
  • 4. Manifestations according to etiology
  • Diagnosis
  • a) Lab tests: Hormone assay: pubertal levels of LH, FSH, E2 (girls) and Testosterone (boys)
  • Basal LH > 0.3 U/L indicates the onset of puberty
  • GnRH stimulation test (stim. with 100 µg GnRH i.v. OR GnRH antagonist → ↑ LH and FSH
  • The LH ↑ after GnRH is used for DD between CPP and prepubertal state
  • b) X-rays of left wrist/hand (bone age determination)
  • c) US of internal genitalia
  • - Increased uterine size and dev. of endometrium & dev. ovarian follicles (girls)
  • - Increased prostate size (boys)
  • d) Cerebral MRI + contrast (to rule out a tumoral; mandatory in both sexes < 6y)
  • Treatment (CPP either idiopathic or neurological)
  • → To suppress sexual maturation and decrease growth rate
  • GnRH agonist causing ↓ secretion of FSH, LH and sex steroids
  • E.g. Triptorelin (DIPHERELINE®) 3.75 mg/vial 1 f/month i.m. (= Depot injection)
  • B. Incomplete PP
  • = premature sexual dvpt in the abscence of premature activation of the HH-gland axis; Ø gametogenesis!
  • Incomplete isosexual PP Incomplete contrasexual PP
  • = the secondary sexual devel. is according
  • to genetic sex
  • FEMALE Source of excessive estrogens - Excess of androgens → masculinization
  • - McCune Albright syndrome E.g. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
  • - Ovarian tumors, follicular cysts
  • MALE - Excess of hCG or LH secreted by tumors - Excess of estrogens → feminization
  • - Excess of androgens (tumors, E.g. Estrogen secreting tumor (adrenal)
  • testotoxicosis)

Delayed Puberty or absent Puberty (Sexual infantilism) #3

  • = any girl of 13 or boy of 14 y. without signs of pubertal development falls >2.5 DS > the mean
  • Classification of delayed puberty
  • 1. Constitutional delay in growth and adolescence
  • = delayed onset of secondary sexual development; delayed skeletal development > 2 SD from the mean
  • - More common in boys
  • - Usually thin, delayed adrenarche and gonadarche
  • - A family history
  • - LH response to exogenous GnRH or an agonist is pubertal
  • - Treatment: observation and psychological support
  • 2. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (defect of HP axis)
  • a) Kallmann syndrome (congenital syndrome with hypogonadism and anosmia)
  • b) Multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies
  • c) Tumors, trauma, irradiation, congenital disorders of hypothalamus or pituitary
  • 3. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
  • a) Klinefelter syndrome
  • b) Turner syndrome
  • → It’s challenging to decide whether the delay is constitutionally or from an organic cause
  • 3. Pituitary Gland: Location and Function
  • - Lies at the base of the skull in the sella turcica within the sphenoid bone
  • - Transversed by CN III, IV, VI, V (ophthalmic branch), internal carotid arteries, optic chiasm
  • - Measures: transversely 13mm, 9mm A/P, 6-9mm vertically; 500-900mg
  • Anterior pituitary - Originates from Rathke pouch
  • (Adenohypophysis) - Ant. pituitary cells = acido-, basophils, chromophobe cells
  • GH + production of IGF-1, actions on growth and metabolism
  • PRL + milk production
  • - gonadotropins secretion
  • ACTH + glucocorticoids and sex steroids in adrenal cortex →
  • inducing adrenal hyperplasia and -trophy of the gland
  • TSH + all aspects of the thyroid function
  • LH ♀ + steroid hormones (androgens)
  • ♂ + steroid hormone production in Leydig cells
  • FSH ♀ targets the granulosa cells to promote follicular development, inhibin
  • secretion
  • ♂ targets the Sertoli cells to promote spermatogenesis, inhibin secretion
  • Posterior pituitary - Neural origin, ventral hypothalamus and 3rd ventricle
  • (Neurohypophysis) Oxyto
  • → explained later cin
  • ADH = vasopressin
  • → All defined pathophysiology is related to vasopressin rather than
  • oxytocin

3.1 Pituitary Disorders #4

  • 3.1.1 The pituitary tumoral syndrome (Pituitary mass effects)
  • = includes the sum of symptoms and signs caused by an expanding pituitary mass into sella turcica or into
  • the suprasellar space
  • Etiology
  • Pituitary adenomas ->95% are benign and monoclonal
  • -Most common cause of HP dysfunction in adults
  • -Great majority is hypersecreting
  • Classification
  • 1.According to tumor size
  • a)Microadenoma: < 1cm, Ø sellar enlargement/ extrasellar extension
  • b)Macroadenoma: > 1cm, causing generalized sellar enlargement
  • 2.According to the state of hormone secretion
  • a)Nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma
  • b)Functioning pituitary adenoma (Prolactinoma)
  • Craniopharyngioma -Originate from metaplasia of resting cells in Rathke pouch
  • Features
  • - ↑ ICP
  • -Visual disturbances
  • -HP disturbances
  • -Growth failure in children
  • -Ant. and post. pituitary failure – incl. diabetes insipidus
  • -Weight gain (due to hyperphagia)
  • Metastatic lesions -CA’s metastizing to hypophysis are breast, lung and GI CA’s
  • Miscellaneous lesions E.g. sarcoidosis, histiocytosis x, lymphomas, pituitary abscess, meningioma
  • Clinical Features
  • -Headache and other neurological signs, pituitary hormone hyper-/ hyposecretion, sellar enlargement,
  • visual loss
  • I.Neurological signs
  • a)Headache = major symptom (due to stretching of the dural plate)
  • -Is frontal, frontoparietal or retro-orbital
  • -Progressive severity; none or only partial painkillers are effective
  • b)Evolution of pituitary masses towards the hypothalamus = hypothalamic syndrome
  • -Disorders of consciousness (e.g. somnolence)
  • -Disorders of behavior
  • -Disorders of thirst and appetite (loss of thirst sensation and hyperphagia; DI)
  • -Disorders of temperature regulation
  • Large pituitary -May extend into cavernous sinus
  • lesions -Compromising CN III, IV, VI
  • →diplopia, palpable ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, ICA compression
  • Very large With both suprasellar and parasellar extension may lead to symptoms of ↑ ICP:
  • pituitary lesions -Severe, persistent headache
  • -Vomiting
  • -Seizures
  • -Bradycardia
  • -Papillary edema = neurosurgery emergencies

II. Ophthalmological signs = neurosurgery emergencies #5

  • → Optic chiasmatic syndrome
  • - Because of the anatomy of the optic chiasm, pressure from below affect temporal visual fields –
  • starting superiorly
  • - Extension to entire temporal field loss = bitemporal hemianopia
  • - Homonymous contralateral hemianopia
  • III. Endocrine and metabolic signs
  • - Signs and symptoms of hyper-/ hyposecretion due to tumoral local pressure
  • Pituitary Hypersecretion ↑↑
  • Prolactinoma - Most common type
  • (57% of primary pituitary tumors) ♀ Amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility
  • ♂ ↓ libido, impotence, infertility
  • GH/GH+PRL secreting pituitary adenoma - Leads to acromegaly and gigantism
  • (10-15%)
  • ACTH secreting pituitary adenoma (5%) - Leads to Cushing DISEASE
  • TSH secreting pituitary adenoma (1%) - Leads to hyperthyroidism with goiter
  • (FSH, LH) gonadotropin secreting - Usual large chromophobe adenomas with:
  • pituitary adenoma (1-2%) - Visual impairment, hypopituitarism, rare: ovarian
  • Hyperstimulation
  • Nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma (28%)
  • Pituitary failure (Hypopituitarism) ↓↓
  • GH Children: short stature
  • Adults: ↓ exercise capacity, ↑ body fat, impaired psychological well-being, ↑ CV risk
  • LH/FSH ♀ Oligo-/ amenorrhea, anovulatory cycles, loss of axillary + pubic hair, osteoporosis
  • ♂ Erectile dysfunction, ↓ libido, testicular atrophy, loss of sexual hair, osteoporosis
  • TSH As in primary hypothyroidism, except lack of goiter
  • ACTH As in Addison’s disease (primary), except lack of hyperpigmentation, hyperkalemia
  • PRL Failure of lactation
  • ADH Polyuria and polydipsia
  • Imaging studies
  • = is the optimal imaging of the pituitary gland and hypothalamus
  • MRI → High resolution T1 in coronal& sagittal planes before + after glandolinium i.v.
  • → The normal gland is 10-12/10/7 mm in its AP/LL/CC
  • → Post. gland appears as “post pituitary bright spot” → absent in pat. with DI
  • → Used for DD
  • Microadenoma (2-9mm) - Low signal intensity compared to normal gland;
  • usually Ø enhance with glandolinium (difficult)
  • → Contrast enhancement, asymmetry of the
  • gland can be helpful in demonstration
  • Macroadenoma (> 10mm) - Readily visualized + definition of extension degree
  • (compression, distorsion, invasion)
  • - ↑ vascularization → ↑ glandolinium affinity
  • CT scan - May be useful for demonstrating calcifications in tumors
  • *Craniopharyngiomas appear as intra- and/or suprasellar masses with cystic
  • and/or solid components; presence of calcifications (45-57%) → better CT/ X-ray
  • Plain skull X-ray - May show pituitary fossa enlargement, but you Ø “see” the the gland

Treatment #6

  • Goals
  • I. Excision of mass
  • II. Suppression/ correction of hormonal hypersecretion
  • III. Preserving the normal secretion of ant. pituitary hormones
  • Surgical Transsphenoidal = procedure of choice
  • treatment microsurgical approach to Microadenoma: complete removal
  • the sella turcica Macroadenoma: partial excision
  • Compl.: post-op hemorrhage, CSF leakage,
  • meningitis, visual impairement, transitory DI
  • Transfrontal/ transparietal - Only for rare invasive suprasellar mass
  • craniotomy extending in the frontal or middle cranial fossa
  • or optic nerve
  • → Frequently major neurological, endocrine
  • complications (DI, pituitary failure, visual
  • impairments
  • Radiotherapy - Reserved for residual mass effect after surgery; contraindicated surgery
  • a) Conventional radiation
  • b) Gamma knife radiosurgery
  • Complications: visual damage, hypopituitarism, seizures, cognitive disorders
  • radionecrosis of brain tissue
  • Pharmacotherapy - Dopamine agonists (Bromocriptine, Cabergoline)
  • → Suppress both PRL and tumor growth in pat. with prolactinoma
  • - Somatostatin analogues = useful for acromegaly, TSH secr. Adenomas, Cushing
  • Posterior pituitary (Neurohypophysis)
  • = Ø a gland; only the distal axon terminals of the hypothalamic magnocellular neurons make up the
  • neurohypophysis
  • Oxytocin ADH (vasopressin)
  • - PRL and oxytocin are the hormones critical to = water-retaining hormone in all mammals
  • lactation - Release occurs in response to osmolality changes
  • + Contraction of myoepithelial cells of mammary - Exercise, nicotine, angiotensin II, high temp.
  • ducts, milk ejection & uterine contraction during ↑ ADH secretion
  • labor - Low temp. and alcohol ↓ ADH secretion
  • Suckling + mechanoreceptors → neurotransmitter - Main site of action: collecting duct and thick
  • trigger release of oxytocin (pulsatile release) → ascending loop of Henle
  • producing a pumping action in the alveoli and - In higher concentration it has a pressor effect
  • max. emptying of milk - Important regulator for plasma osmolality,
  • - Oxytocin release is + by visual, psychological or water balance, arterial pressure
  • physical stimuli (prepare the mother for feeding)
  • - PRL release is limited to suckling reflex arch!
  • - Most specific role of oxy: release of oxy brought
  • about by vaginal & cervical dilatation; + max.
  • uterine muscle contraction & clamp down blood
  • vessels to ↓ blood loss
  • - Oxy receptor inhib. can delay delivery ≈ 24-48h
  • - No known role of oxytocin for ♂

3.1.2 Diabetes insipidus (DI) #7

  • = failure to secrete adequate quantities of ADH or the failure of the kidney to respond to circulating ADH
  • → Excretion of large volumes of urine that is hypotonic, (< 300 mOsm/kg) diluted and tasteless
  • Classification
  • a) According to the site of lesions (central/ nephrogenic)
  • b) According to duration (transitory/ permanent)
  • Etiology
  • Central DI - Craniopharyngioma (most common solid tumor)
  • - Surgery in hypothalamic, pit. stalk region
  • - Head trauma
  • - Infiltrative disorders: sarcoidosis, histiocytes, lymphomas
  • - Infections: meningitis, meningoencephalitis
  • - Autoimmune
  • - DIDMOAD syndrome (DI + DM + optic atrophy + deafness = Wolfram syndr.)
  • - Idiopathic
  • Nephrogenic DI Acquired: CKD - interferes with collecting duct or medullary function
  • Hypokalemia, hypercalcemia
  • Drugs: Lithium, demeclocycline
  • Familial: X-linkes recessive – vasopressin receptor gene/ aquaporin-2 gene
  • Clinical features
  • Adults: polyuria, nocturia, thirst, polydipsia
  • Children: polyuria, enuresis and failure to thrive
  • Rarely: acute dehydration characterized by arterial hypotension, shock and coma
  • Diagnosis
  • 1. Confirm large urine output (> 3L/day) with low urinary density (< 1.005)
  • 2. Exclude DM and renal failure as well as electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, hypercalcemia)
  • 3. Dehydration test
  • - NO fluids for 12-18h; measure body weight, BP, pulse, urine flow, urine specific gravity each hour;
  • Urine and plasma osmolality
  • → In DI urine flow remains ↑, while urine specific density is ↓ (<1.005) and urine osmolality remains
  • <300 mOsm/kg ►►► PATIENT BECOMES DEHYDRATED
  • 4. ADH radioimmunoassay
  • - Usually measured at the end of the Dehydration test; levels are LOW in CENTRAL DI and
  • levels are HIGH in NEPHROGENIC DI
  • 5. Vasopressin test (for DD central/nephrogenic)
  • 5 units of vasopressin parentally or 2 µg of desmopressin and then measuring urinary flow and density
  • for 2 more hours:
  • Urinary flow Urinary density & osmolality
  • Central DI ↓ ↑
  • Nephrogenic DI remains ↑ ↓
  • Imaging studies
  • I. MRI head
  • - Looking for tumors
  • → May demonstrate loss of post. bright spot of the post. pituitary gland

II. Abdominal US, i.v. urography #8

  • - For renal pathology
  • DD of Polyuria-Polydipsia syndrome
  • - Primary polydipsia = ↑ drinking in excess of 5L/day → dilution of extracellular fluid, inhibition of
  • ADH secretion, water diuresis
  • → It’s a disorder of thirst that is either due to psychogenic cause or to altered osmotic and
  • nonosmotic regulations of thirst
  • - Other causes of polyuria: CRF (polyuric phase), DM, hypercalcemia (impairment of renal
  • concentration), hypokalemia (NaKCl2 cotransport; impared responsiveness to ADH)
  • Treatment:
  • Central DI Hormonal treatment of substitution:
  • →Desmopressin acetate
  • =Vasopressin analogue, acting predominantly on the V2 receptors in the kidney
  • →Drug may be administered in divided doses,
  • orally Minirin ®(100–1,000 micrograms/day),
  • intranasally (10–40 micrograms/day),
  • parenterally (SC, IV, IM) (0.1–2 micrograms/day)
  • sublingually.- Minirin melt ®60-120 µg 3times/day sublingual
  • Etiologic treatment: the underlying disorder should be treated if possible
  • Nephrogenic •Correction of underlying cause (metabolic or drugs)
  • DI •Maintenance of adequate fluid input
  • •High doses of desmopressin (e.g. up to 5 micrograms IM) can be effective
  • •Thiazide diuretics- Hydroclorothiazide (NEFRIX) 25-50 mg/day+ low sodium diet
  • → encourages salt and water uptake in proximal tubule

3.1.3 Acromegaly and gigantism #9

  • = classical syndromes of GH-secreting adenomas (2nd in frequency to prolactinomas)
  • - Classical features (overgrowth of bone) are due to chronic excessive GH and hence IGF-1 secretion
  • Adults → Acromegaly → Local overgrowth of bone (skull, mandible); Ø
  • linear growth due to prior fusion of long bone
  • epiphysis
  • Childhood/ Adolescence (prior epiphyseal → Associated hypogonadism, delayed
  • fusion) → Gigantism epiphyseal closure + striking acceleration of
  • linear growth (height >+3 SD for age and sex)
  • → Can also have acromegaly features, if the GH
  • hypersecretion persists through adolescence
  • and into adulthood
  • GH and IGF-1 effects and pathophysiology of acromegaly
  • 1. Growth promoting
  • - Chronic GH hypersecretion due to excessive amounts of IGF-1
  • - IGF-1 has growth promoting effects (charact. proliferation of bone, cartilage, soft tissue and ↑ organ
  • size)
  • 2. Metabolic effects
  • → carbohydrate, lipid, phosphocalcic, hydroelectric metabolisms
  • a) GH → insulin resistance and carbohydrate intolerance
  • b) GH has also direct effects on → lipid, phosphocalcic, hydroelectric metabolisms → lipolysis,
  • hypercalciuria, ↑ renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate, sodium and water
  • Etiology
  • 1. GH secreting pituitary adenoma or mixed GH-PRL secreting pituitary adenoma
  • → Acromegaly and gigantism are virtually always secondary to a pituitary adenoma
  • - Several syndromes are associated with pit. adenomas and GH hypersecretion
  • → MEN type 1 (Werner syndrome) = isolated GH-secreting pituitary adenoma, primary
  • hyperparathyroidism, pancreatic tumors (gastrinomas, islet cell tumors)
  • → MEN type 4 (MEN X) = parathyroid and ant. pituitary tumors, possible adrenal, kidney and
  • reproductive organ tumors
  • → McCune Albright syndrome =fibrous bone dysplasia, café-au-lait pigmentation, gland
  • dysfunction → regulating the growth, sexual development and metabolic functions
  • → Carney complex = clinically: lentigines, myxomas (cardiac), tumors + schwannomas
  • - Familial acromegaly/ gigantism
  • - X-linked acrogigantism
  • - Neurofibromatosis (very rare, NF1)
  • - Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome = hereditary tumors (cornea, spinal cord, kidney, adrenals, pancreas)
  • - Familial isolated pituitary adenomas (FIPA)
  • - By genetic defects in the aryl hydrocarbon receptor interacting protein (AIP), probably act as tumor
  • suppressor
  • a) The existence of ≥2 cases of acromegaly/ gigantism in a family Ø MEN 1 or Carney complex
  • b) 30-50% have a mutation in AIP gene
  • c) Early onset of the disease (< 30y.)
  • d) Poor response to somatostatin analogues
  • e) Take a careful family history → screening for AIP; family history may Ø be positive → low penetrance

2. Paraneoplastic secretion of GHRH-like/ GH-like substances #10

  • a) Ectopic production of GHRH → pituitary somatotroph hyperplasia (lung CA, islet cell tumor)
  • b) Ectopic GH secretion (only a few cases) by a malignant islet tumor, NHL
  • Clinical features of acromegaly
  • Acrofacial dysmorphism Combination of bone + soft tissue overgrowth → typical facies
  • - Face and skull changes: thickening of calvarium, ↑ size of
  • frontal sinuses → frontal bossing, enlargement of nose,
  • downward and forward growth of mandible → prognathism
  • - Dental problems (teeth separation, overbite)
  • - Soft tissue growth: macroglossia, facial and infraorbital
  • puffiness, voice deepening (laryngeal n. hypertrophyn
  • enlarged paranasal sinuses)
  • - Skeletal hypertrophy: hands + feet (repeated resizing of rings/
  • shoes)
  • - Generalized thickening of skin, ↑ oiliness and sweating, acne
  • - ♀ acanthosis nigricans of axillae and neck, hyperthrichiosis
  • Articular & neural manifestations = Acromegalic arthropathy
  • - Bone and cartilage overgrowth → arthralgia
  • - Long standing cases → degener. arthritis of spine, knees, hip
  • - Spinal involvement includes: osteophytosis, disc space
  • widening, dorsal kyphosis
  • - Carpal tunnel syndrome (neural enlargement, wrist tissue
  • swelling) characterized by painful median n. compression
  • Respiratory manifestations - Sleep apnea (obstructive and central)
  • - Prognathism, thick lips, macroglossia, hypertrophied
  • nasopharyngeal structures → important for tracheal intubation
  • - Narcolepsy, habitual excessive snoring
  • GH excess leads to generalized - Thyromegaly
  • visceromegaly - Enlargement of salivary glands
  • - Enlargement of other organs (heart, kidney, liver) usually
  • NOT clinically detectable
  • Gastrointestinal manifestations - Constipation → long and tortuous colon → can lead to rectal
  • Prolapse
  • - Colonic polyps: pat. >40 y. should have a routine colonoscopy
  • Cardiovascular manifestations - Major cause of morbidity and mortality
  • - Arterial hypertension
  • - LVH
  • - Cardiac enlargement → secondary to hypertension
  • Other endocrine and metabolism - Diffuse or nodular goiter
  • abnormalities - Galactorrhea/ gynecomastia
  • - DM/ IGT
  • - Hypertriglyceridemia type 4
  • - Hyperlipoproteinemia
  • - Hypercalciuria
  • - Nephrolithiasis
  • Systemic manifestation - Lethargy, fatigue
  • - Weight gain
  • - Hyperhidrosis and heat intolerance

Clinical investigations of acromegaly #11

  • 1.Lab (hormonal) findings
  • A.GH-IGF-1 Axis-Basal determinations and dynamic tests
  • -GH levels vary according to age (normal range 1-5 ng/ml)
  • →basal fasting GH > 10ng/ml in > 90% of patients
  • →A single random measurement is not entirely reliable, because GH secretion can be influenced by other
  • causes, such as:
  • ↑ GH secretion -Exercise
  • -Sleep
  • -Stress (physical, psychological)
  • -Hypoglycemia
  • ↓ GH secretion -Postprandial hyperglycemia elevated FFA
  • →Suppression with oral glucose is the simplest and most specific dynamic test for acromegaly
  • B.Glucose suppression test
  • -75g oral glucose with GH determination at 0, 30 and 60 minutes
  • Interpretation: healthy subjects → reduction of GH level to < 1ng/ml at 60 min.
  • →Acromegaly: HG levels may decrease, increase or show no change
  • →The failure to suppress GH < 1ng/ml after 60 min. establishes the diagnosis
  • C.IGF-1 measurements
  • 2.PRL measurement
  • -Serum PRL should be measured because some tumors co-secrete GH and PRL
  • 3.Evaluation of pituitary reserve
  • -FSH, LH, estradiol/testosterone, TSH/FT4, ACTH/cortisol
  • →assessment of ant. pituitary gland function
  • Imaging studies
  • MRI/ CT scan of pituitary fossa -Following the biochemical diagnosis → visualization of tumor
  • size and appearance + parasellar extent
  • -MRI (before + after gadolinium administration) = imaging of
  • choice for hypothalamus and pituitary gland
  • Lateral plain films of skull →focused on sella turcica → sellar enlargement
  • With the X-Rays we cant see the +thickening of calvarium, enlargement of frontal sinuses,
  • tumor, only signs of Acromegalia prognathism, hypertrophy of ant. clinoids = “acromegalic beak”
  • X-ray of hand -↑ soft tissue bulk
  • -‘’arrowhead ‘’ tufting of the distal phalanges
  • RX feet: similar changes and there is ↑
  • -↑ width of intraarticular cartilages
  • thickness of the heel pad (normal <22mm )
  • -Cystic changes of carpal bones
  • Ophthalmologic investigations
  • -Visual field test → when tumor is found about the optic chiasm; bitemporal hemianopsia, unexplained
  • visual flied defects or loss
  • Others (associated with comorbidities)
  • -Thyroid and abdominal US (→ visceromegaly)
  • -Colonoscopy (→ polyps, colon CA)
  • -Ca2+ and phosphorus metabolism (→ ↑ serum phosphorus, hypercalciuria, ↑ alkaline phosphatase)
  • -Carbohydrate metabolism (→ DM/ IGT)

-EKG/ echorcardiography → LVH or global hypertrophy, cardiomegaly, allows evaluation for s #12

  • (low ejection fraction) or diastolic ventricular impairment (heart failure)
  • Complications
  • -Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases
  • -Sleep apnea
  • -Acromegalic arthropathy with progressive cosmetic deformity and degenerative arthritis
  • -Colonic CA
  • -Neurological complications (carpal tunnel syndrome)
  • -Nephrolithiasis
  • Treatment
  • Goals: to halt progression and prevent late complications; removal/ destruction of tumor, maintenance of
  • normal ant. pituitary function
  • 1.Surgical treatment
  • craniotomy is necessary in the rare patients in whom the major suprasellar
  • = transsphenoidal surgery → usually 1st line treatment and lateral extension precludes the transsphenoidal approach
  • -After surgery measuring an IGF-1 level and a random GH at 12 weeks or later (> 1µg/l is suggested)
  • -Pat. with persistent GH hypersecretion after surgery should receive medical and/or radiotherapy
  • treatment
  • 2.Medical treatment
  • Drugs that counteract Somatostatin = SST receptor ligands (SRLs)
  • GH-IGF-1 hypersecretion analogues -Therapy of choice for residual GH
  • hypersecretion
  • -May be used as primary therapy for
  • macroadenomas (> 2cm) or unacceptable
  • surgery/ anesthesia risk

5. The Parathyroid Gland #36

  • 5.1 Calcium and bone metabolism Hormones involved in the calcium metabolism regulation
  • Role of calcium
  • - Bone building

  • - Neuromuscular conduction

  • → The bones contain approx. 99.5% of the total calcium in the body
  • Circulated calcium
  • a) Ionized → biologically active (50%)
  • b) Complexed to citrate, phosphate etc. → biologically active (5%)
  • c) Bound to protein, mainly albumin → inactive (45%)
  • In most clinical situations → important to adjust the measured calcium (- albumin)
  • Adjusted Ca2+ = measured Ca mmol/L + 0.02 x (40- albumin g/L)
  • Ca2+ regulating hormones (PTH, CT, Vit. D + metabolites)
  • 1. PTH
  • - Central function: regulate ionized Ca2+ on 3 target organs: bone, intestinal mucosa, kidney
  • - PTH is secreted from 4 glands; 2 superior and 2 inferior
  • - Normal parathyroid glands weigh ≈ 40 mg each
  • Biological effects
  • Kidney: PTH has direct effects; ↑ Ca reabsorption in DCT, ↓ reabsorption of phosphate in prox. tubule,
  • stimulation of calcitriol (= 1,25(OH)²D³ = Vit D3) synthesis
  • Intestinal mucosa: indirect effect on intestinal Ca reabsorption resulting from ↑ renal production of
  • intestinally active Vit D metabolite (Calcitriol)
  • Bone: PTH ↑ both bone formation and bone resorption (resorption is dominant)
  • 2. Calcitonin (CT)
  • = secreted by parafollicular C cells of the thyroid
  • Biological effects
  • Bone: CT inhibits osteoclastic-mediated bone resorption (main function)
  • Kidney: CT inhibits resorption of phosphate and ↑ renal excretion of Ca2+
  • CT is Ø measured routinely; 2 interests: a) important tumor marker in medullary thyroid CA; b)
  • therapeutic uses as inhibitor of osteoclastic bone resorption → treatment of Paget’s disease, hyperCa2+,
  • osteoporosis

  • - Main function of this metabolites is regulation of Ca2+ and phosphate homeostasis
